chapter: The union and the 1920s-30s band scene
title: The Momart in Hollywood and Howard's caution about what gets said
summary: Willard asks about the Momart; Howard says much is left out of the books and explains why he stays clear of certain people.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Was this before or after the Quality Serenaders played the Montmartre in Hollywood?
That's what (inaudible). That's the Momart. Yeah.
I saw a picture in that book that said the Momart.
Momart, right.
And I've heard of the Momart in Hollywood.
See, that's what I want to do because there's a lot of things they're leaving out.
What?
Lot of things --
That's all right. They'll come together later. Because you'll begin to hear the tape and then maybe you can fit in some other things.
Maybe so.
You might ask Florence. She would know about that, although she wasn't working at the time.
Florence(unintelligible)? (Unintelligible?)
Yeah.
Shewould know a lot about that, wouldn't she?
Well, she'd know something, not a whole lot.
(Laughter.)
I like the way you said that.
Well, no, I don't want to see you go get yourself out in the cold and can't get back in.
Oh, yeah. I'm not going to do that. That's why I'm sticking with you.
(Laughter)

I ain't going to get out there because I know what those people are doing and what they're thinking and what they say. And they're all friends of mine. Nice people, too. And I love them all, but I'm not going to get out there. My wife, she's kind of -- she steps out there, but I ain't going out there. I know what they do, see. If they

don't treat you nice, they have a way of crushing you. They're Not going to crush me, because I know my way in this town and I've been here years and years and years and years. And I'm happy to be here, and happy to know you. And I know you and you wouldn't give me two thoughts if I wasn't a gentleman. That's the truth. You wouldn't.
